source.title: Scaling Collaborative Effort with Agents
source.authors: Shannon Zejiang Shen; Valerie Chen; Ken Gu; Alexis Ross; Zixian Ma; Jillian Ross; Alex Gu; Chenglei Si; Wayne Chi; Andi Peng; Jocelyn J. Shen; A. Talwalkar; Tong-Shuang Wu; David A. Sontag

record.tranche_reason: The paper says its collaborative-effort framework takes inspiration from machine-learning scaling laws, but it does not test pretraining-loss scaling or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as inspiration for a framework about agent utility as user involvement increases. Its travel-planning results concern simulated collaboration, not held-out pretraining loss as a function of model parameters, tokens, or compute. The one row records the related but different agent-performance trajectory; it does not test a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only as inspiration for a 'collaborative effort scaling' framework. It measures travel-plan quality of prompted agents (claude-3.5/4.0-sonnet, gpt-4o, llama-3.1-70b) against simulated-user interaction rounds. It does not measure pretraining loss, parameters, tokens, compute, or downstream performance against model scale, and it does not use any scaling law as a working tool. So it neither tests nor uses the claim (T6, not T4).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Fuller version: the authors argue that agents should be evaluated by how their utility scales with user effort ('collaborative effort scaling'). In simulated travel planning, current agents are mediocre collaborators: extra user effort often brings little gain over autonomous baselines. Collaboration scaffolds (one-stage vs two-stage planning) matter in model-dependent ways.
record.recipe_differences: No original scaling-law fitting or training-size/compute sweep is performed; scaling laws are cited as inspiration for a collaboration-evaluation framework.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that collaborative performance varies by underlying model and by one-stage versus two-stage planning strategy; these are not tests of pretraining-loss scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: In simulated travel planning, agent plan quality rises over the first rounds and plateaus after about five rounds for all agents. For gpt-4o and llama-3.1-70b, collaboration does not beat the autonomous baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agent utility in human-agent collaboration saturates quickly with user effort (interaction rounds) rather than scaling steadily.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
record.problems: The experiments use simulated users and focus in depth on a single task domain, but the study does not provide evidence about the listed pretraining-scaling claims.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports additional travel-planning utility and usability metrics by model and collaboration strategy; they do not measure any listed claim version and are not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
No other modality or training regime examined for power-law loss.
Models of different capability are compared, but scale is not stated or varied, so there is no downstream-versus-scale relation.
No exponents or fitting choices analysed.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4/uses_without_test is changed to cites_only/T6. Scaling laws serve only as an analogy and are not used as a working tool.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits on small pretraining runs or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation of model parameters and training tokens.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No modality or training-regime comparison of pretraining-loss scaling.
No test of downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No analysis of pretraining-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves.

rows.subject: all tested agents
rows.operation_detail: Measured travel-plan performance over successive rounds of simulated agent-user collaboration.
rows.value: Performance improves at the beginning of collaboration and plateaus after around five rounds for all agents.
rows.note: This is collaborative agent performance versus user-interaction rounds, not language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
rows.check: The row measures agent performance against user-interaction rounds, not any claim version, so state against a version cannot be read. As a descriptive finding the plateau after about five rounds is reported correctly (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
